Week 73: A Week Balanced on the Edge

Unauthorized war-making, loyalist appointments, and diverted funds met courts, senators, and a jury that mostly held the line.

Week 73 opens on a familiar unease. Nothing in these seven days announced itself as a rupture. Instead, the period moved the way most of this term has moved lately: through small tests against institutions that mostly, but not always, held. The clock's near-stillness this week does not mean nothing happened. It means the pressure and the resistance came, for once, close to balanced.

At the close of the previous period, the clock stood at 7:41 p.m. It closed Week 73 at the same public time, a net movement of six-tenths of a minute toward erosion, so small it barely registers on the clock's face. That stillness is not calm. Beneath it sat a week of unauthorized war-making, loyalist appointments, diverted public funds, and family enrichment, all pressing in one direction. Courts that ruled, senators who balked, and a jury that acquitted pushed back almost exactly hard enough to offset it. The mechanism did not freeze. It strained both ways and barely moved.

The clearest and most serious thread ran through the Iran crisis. On June 9, a helicopter went down near the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump ordered retaliatory strikes. Two days later he announced a fresh round of strikes, then cancelled them within hours, citing a diplomatic breakthrough. Iranian state media, the Pakistani prime minister, and the president himself described that breakthrough in three incompatible ways. By week's end, General Dan Caine had reportedly briefed him in secret on a plan for ground invasion, aimed at seizing Iran's enriched uranium. No vote authorized any of it. No public account matched any other.

The economic shock of this improvisation was immediate and measurable. Oil prices jumped with each escalation. Producer prices rose 6.5 percent year over year, the highest reading since 2022. Oil executives privately warned the White House that gasoline could reach five dollars a gallon, even as the president publicly claimed to love inflation. War conducted this way risks more than lives. It corrodes the public's ability to plan, to trust prices, to know what its government is doing in its name.

A second thread ran through the machinery of law enforcement and intelligence. Trump nominated Todd Blanche, his own former defense attorney, as permanent Attorney General, merging personal loyalty with the nation's chief prosecutorial office. At the same time, he tried to install Bill Pulte, a wealthy ally with no qualifications, as acting Director of National Intelligence. This time the response was not silence. Three Republican senators joined Democrats to block Pulte outright. The nomination collapsed under bipartisan weight, replaced by Jay Clayton, himself entangled in the slow release of the Epstein files.

The fight over the intelligence directorship carried a cost nobody intended. Because it dragged past deadline, the House failed to extend FISA Section 702, and a major surveillance authority lapsed for the first time in years. This was not a deliberate curtailment of state power; it was collateral damage from a fight over who should hold it. Meanwhile, mass departures from the FBI, and Hegseth's unexplained purge of women and Black nominees from the Navy's promotion list, deepened concern that the civil service is being hollowed into a loyalty apparatus rather than a professional one.

Public money moved toward private glory again this week, in several forms at once. DOJ briefly revived a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund it had itself declared dead. Trump declined to rule out using it to pay people convicted of assaulting police on January 6. Separately, $352 million in Secret Service funds was redirected to the White House ballroom project, after Trump had promised private financing and Congress had refused to approve it directly. At least $60 million in federal resources went toward staging a UFC event on White House grounds, tied to Trump's own financial stake in the sport.

Each of these efforts met resistance, and in most cases resistance won or held. Judge Leonie Brinkema extended her injunction against the anti-weaponization fund and later made it preliminary. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued over the ballroom project. A separate suit tried to stop the UFC event, though Judge Amit Mehta declined to intervene on timing grounds and let it proceed. The pattern here is not unchecked executive will. It is an executive testing the same boundary again and again, and courts pushing back, not always successfully, but consistently.

Family enrichment deepened alongside these disputes. Jared Kushner's investment firm received two billion dollars from Saudi Arabia while he remained active in Middle East diplomacy. His and Trump's business interests advanced a $1.9 billion luxury resort on protected Albanian wetlands, drawing over 150,000 protesters into the streets of a foreign capital. An Indian conglomerate invested at least $100 million in a startup linked to Donald Trump Jr., timed alongside tariff and sanctions relief for the same interests. Trump Jr.'s own net worth rose from roughly fifty million dollars to three hundred million since the 2024 election. None of this required a crime. It required only proximity.

The judiciary, tested from multiple directions, mostly held its ground. Judge Leo Sorokin struck down Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax requiring congressional authorization. Judge Christopher Cooper's order that the Kennedy Center remove Trump's name survived a denied stay at the D.C. Circuit, even as the Center's board threatened bankruptcy through an emergency bylaw change rather than comply. Judge Boasberg declined to vacate his protection of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell from a politically charged grand jury subpoena. Each ruling reaffirmed a distinct boundary: taxation, congressional funding authority, and the independence of monetary policy. The DOJ made a separate argument this week, that courts have no power to review executive demolition of federal property after the fact. That claim shows what the alternative theory of power actually wants. It did not win. It will return.

Immigration enforcement kept expanding its reach as transparency declined. ICE abandoned a policy requiring it to report detainee deaths within thirty days of release, even as deaths in custody rose. A separate scheme reportedly moved to falsely mark 2.7 million immigrants as dead in federal records to induce self-deportation. Nearly all refugee admissions this period, 6,665 of 6,668, were white South Africans. ICE detained roughly 500 infants and toddlers and apprehended the parents of some 14,450 U.S.-born children. At Delaney Hall, detained women began a hunger strike over conditions and were met with cancelled visitations and transfers. Protesters outside met tear gas and mass arrests.

Congress, for its part, chose to fund this apparatus without reforming it. The Secure America Act locked in $70 billion for ICE and CBP through 2029, passed without Democratic votes and without oversight conditions. In the Senate, Republicans blocked amendments that would have barred the slush fund, prevented Pulte's dual-agency leadership, and restricted unapproved ballroom spending. The effect is durable. Years of enforcement funding now sit beyond the easy reach of any future Congress to condition or claw back.

Press freedom absorbed its own quiet damage. CBS fired veteran correspondent Scott Pelley after he refused editorial pressure to falsify a story to fit the administration's preferred narrative. Editorial director Bari Weiss reportedly sought to misstate the facts of a fatal ICE shooting. Days earlier, Trump had walked out of a Meet the Press interview rather than answer for his unsubstantiated claims of fraud in the Los Angeles mayoral primary. These are not unrelated incidents. They describe pressure from two directions at once: an executive that punishes journalists who ask hard questions, and a network willing to punish journalists who answer them honestly.

Voter suppression rhetoric hardened into something closer to structural effort. Multiple Fox hosts and Republican officials sustained baseless claims that California's election was rigged. Vance echoed the same claims about slow ballot counting. Trump pressured Senate Majority Leader Thune to remove the Senate Parliamentarian after she ruled a voting-restriction bill violated procedural rules. The FBI raided a voter-participation nonprofit on a fraud pretext so rare it borders on nonexistent. Separately, the administration floated postal rules that could let the Postal Service refuse to deliver mail ballots in states that withhold voter rolls. No single action changed an election outcome this week. Together, they describe an infrastructure being prepared.

Not every current ran toward erosion. Brad Lander, the former New York City comptroller, was fully acquitted of obstruction charges stemming from his peaceful inspection of an ICE facility, a judicial rejection of the pattern that treats oversight as criminal disorder. Judge Emily Marks permanently barred Alabama from executing a death row inmate by nitrogen gas, reaffirming a constitutional limit on state punishment. A Brooklyn jury convicted a defendant of a hate-motivated killing under ordinary criminal process. These were not large victories. They were proof that ordinary legal process still functions when tested directly.

FISA's lapse, still unresolved at week's end, is the clearest open question carried forward. So is the fate of the anti-weaponization fund, now under sustained injunction but not yet closed for good, and the confirmation fight still pending for Blanche at the Justice Department. None of these threads concluded this week. They were extended, contested, and left for the weeks ahead to settle.

What Week 73 shows, more than any single event within it, is how close to balance a democracy under sustained pressure can still sit. The erosion did not pause because the pressure eased. It paused because resistance, this week, matched it almost exactly: three senators who would not confirm an unqualified nominee, judges who would not lift an injunction, a jury that would not convict a man for bearing witness. The mechanism held, but only barely, and only because enough people inside it still chose to hold their ground. That is not victory. It is the shape of a system still capable of friction, still able to make power answer for what it wants to take.
